questions.question: What is a subspace $U\subseteq V$?
options: A nonempty subset of $V$ that contains the zero vector.
A subset of $V$ that is itself a vector space.
Any subset of $V$ closed under vector addition.
A subset of $V$ of strictly smaller dimension.

questions.question: What closure properties are required for a subset to be a subspace?
options: Closure under addition and additive inverses only.
Closure under addition and positive scalar multiples.
Closure under scalar multiplication only.
Closure under addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.question: If $U$ and $W$ are subspaces of a vector space $V$, which statement about $U\cap W$ is guaranteed?
options: never a subspace
a subspace only if $U\subseteq W$
the empty set
always a subspace of $V$

questions.question: Is the union $U\cup W$ of two subspaces always a subspace?
options: No, unless one is contained in the other
Yes, since each part is closed under addition
Yes, provided the two subspaces meet only in $0$
No; it is a subspace only when $U=W$

questions.question: Is the $x$-axis $\{(x,0)\colon x\in\mathbb{R}\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No; a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$ must contain both $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.
No; it is not closed under multiplication by negative scalars.
Yes; it contains $(0,0)$ and is closed under both operations.
Yes, because every line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a subspace.

questions.question: Is $\{(x,y)\colon x+y=1\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: Yes, it is a line in the plane.
No, it does not contain $(0,0)$.
No, because it contains too many vectors.
Yes, it is closed under every scalar multiplication.

questions.question: Is $\{(x,y)\colon x \gt 0\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No; $(0,0)$ is missing and $-1\cdot(1,0)$ leaves the set.
No; it is not closed under addition of its vectors.
Yes; it is closed under addition and positive scaling.
No, but $\{(x,y)\colon x\ge0\}$ would be a subspace.

questions.question: Is $\{(0,0)\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No, because it has only one vector.
Yes, because every singleton subset is a subspace.
Yes, it is the zero subspace.
No, because subspaces must be infinite.

questions.question: Is $U=\{(x,y,z)\colon z=0\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$?
options: No; it is the solution set of an equation, not a span.
No; a two-dimensional plane cannot be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
Yes, because every subset containing the zero vector is a subspace.
Yes, it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.question: Why is $\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2)$ a subspace?
options: It contains only the two listed vectors and nothing else.
It is a subspace only if $v_1$ and $v_2$ are linearly independent.
Its elements $av_1+bv_2$ are closed under addition and scaling.
It contains $0$, $v_1$ and $v_2$, which is all a subspace needs.

questions.question: A subset $U$ of a vector space contains a vector $\boldsymbol{u}$ but not $2\boldsymbol{u}$. Can $U$ be a subspace?
options: Yes, provided $U$ contains the zero vector.
No, because a subspace containing $\boldsymbol{u}$ must equal $\operatorname{span}(\boldsymbol{u})$.
No, closure under scalar multiplication fails.
It depends on whether other multiples such as $3\boldsymbol{u}$ lie in $U$.

questions.question: A nonempty subset $U$ of $V$ satisfies $\alpha\boldsymbol{u}_1+\beta\boldsymbol{u}_2\in U$ for all $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\boldsymbol{u}_2\in U$ and all scalars $\alpha,\beta$. Which choice in this condition shows directly that $\boldsymbol{0}\in U$?
options: $\alpha=\beta=0$, with any $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\boldsymbol{u}_2\in U$
$\alpha=\beta=1$, with any $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\boldsymbol{u}_2\in U$
$\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0$, with any $\boldsymbol{u}_1,\boldsymbol{u}_2\in U$
None; $\boldsymbol{0}\in U$ must be checked as a separate condition
